subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW

speechtext: Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved the second reading of Bill No. 47, to amend the War Service Grants Act, 1944.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext: Is the minister making a statement on this bill?	.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the War Service Grants Act provided for a board of five to review and examine the service records of those men classified as having been discharged from the forces with what is defined by the services as dishonourable discharge. It was intended that this board should see if there were any mitigating circumstances, in which case the board would have the power and would advocate payment of war service gratuity and the setting up of re-establishment credits.
The board began its work with the Department of Veterans Affairs in February, 1946, and up to February 29, 1948, completed a total of 7,879 cases. Of that number, 5,035 were given favourable decisions and 2,844 have been finally refused entitlement. Some 458 cases remain to be reviewed, and it is considered that this should not take very long. The department foresees a condition coming up shortly when it will be more economical and as satisfactory to establish a reviewing officer within the department to perform the few remaining functions formerly exercised by the board. It should be noted, I think, that, while this board has authority to interpret with respect to entitlement for re-establishment benefits, it had and has no right to change the record of a man's service. It merely considered each case with a view to advocating award of the gratuity or re-establishment credit.
At this time, with the approaching end of the work of the board, I should like to pay tribute to their approach to that work and the way in which they have executed a difficult task with understanding and humanity. I can assure the committee that from what I have seen of the work of the board its members have leaned backward to give the benefit of the doubt in all cases. In saying that, I think,

too, one should say it is a tribute to our Canadian forces in this war when, after being sifted by an impartial group of their peers and equals, that small group of less than -03 per cent have not been considered entitled to Canada's re-establishment benefits.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext: Is it the intention that the present board will review all cases which remain undecided?

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext: Yes, that is the intention. I am prepared to meet the wishes of the committee as to whether or not this bill should be referred to the committee on veterans affairs.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Abolition of board of review.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext: Are the rejections in the two thousand cases final, or would they be on hand if in the odd case an appeal were made?

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext: Those are final as at this date. It was thought that a member of the department would have under constant review any new evidence coming to light at any time.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext: Has consideration been given to setting up within the department a board of officials of the department who would make these decisions, instead of leaving it to one person? The powers are wide and these are important questions. I doubt whether it would be wise to leave them to one man. Surely some of the senior officials in the department could be constituted a board to deal with the few cases which may come up from time to time. It would not be necessary to have them paid for that work; it would be just another job for them. I suggest that this would be more sensible than the present provision which gives to one man in the department the job of reviewing all these cases, and makes his word law. Surely it is not wise to give one man all that power. The amendment gets away from the judicial function. This one man will become the employee of the department whose job it is to go over these cases. My suggestion is that we should have a board acting as a judicial body.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext:
I agree in the main with what the hon. member says. As is shown in the bill, the board is still in existence. This is enabling authority to carry forward any further work when the main task of the board disappears.
In the preliminary discussions respecting the carrying-through technique to be applied afterwards, something along the lines suggested by the hon. member has been discussed. We will keep that situation in mind. In

Private Bills
other words, I can assure the committee that in the continuation of the work this official will be looked upon more as a person detailed to study cases, but that each case will come before the deputy minister and/or a committee created under him as the most effective means of carrying out the purpose of the bill.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext:
But that is not the way the section reads. The proposed amendment refers to abolishing the board of review and transferring its powers, duties and functions to an officer employed in the Department of Veterans Affairs, who shall be called the "'Reviewing Officer, War Service Grants Act". This officer "shall exercise and perform such powers, duties and functions in accordance with rules of procedure to be made by the governor in council." In other words, the amendment gives this employee full power, and there is nowhere any suggestion that the deputy minister or any other senior officials are to review decisions of this "Reviewing Officer, War Service Grants Act".
Could not section 12B in the act be left as it now stands? It provides for the appointment of a board of review and also states that the members are to receive such remuneration as the governor in council may determine. The minister could set up a board of review composed of his senior officials. They need not be paid any remuneration for this work, because there would be very few cases. In this way we would have a judicial board. Under the proposed amendment, one employee in the department, in effect becomes the board, and has all the powers given by the act.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext: I may be wrong, but I can see no reason why the objective sought by the hon. member could not be carried out, if this amendment were accepted.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext:
If the amendment passes, a veteran who has been deprived of his war service grant can appeal only to this officer; he cannot appeal to a board such as is described in the act.
The minister has intimated his intention to have some of the senior officers review the work of the reviewing officer. If that is so, then surely this amendment is superfluous. The proper procedure would be to appoint a board composed of senior officials with authority to do the reviewing. The preliminary work could be done by an employee of the board, but the final decision ivould be made by the senior officials.
I am certain that that is what the veterans would prefer, namely, to have the final decision made by a board rather than by one
man. Would the minister be willing to consider this during the supper recess with his officials?

subtopic: ABOLITION OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext:
I shall do that.
Section stands.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Under the circumstances, since the hon. member did not hear what I said owing to some noise ini the chamber, I think he should be allowed to speak.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Why do these bills from the senate always have the same movers in this house? One hon. member has several bills ini his name. I object to the procedure with respect to these private bills. They are introduced in the senate and, after little or no discussion there, they are sent over here. It is becoming a racket if you ask me. I have followed these proceedings for the last month. The bill is introduced and read the first and second times in the senate, with hardly anybody there, and there is no discussion. Once in a while a bill is sent to a committee, where the whole discussion occupies only three or four lines, and then the bill is sent over here. The bill should be introduced here where the people's representatives are.
The present procedure is a farce and a racket. What discussion is there upon the second reading of the bill? How many of these insurance companies have we? Has the superintendent of insurance reported on this bill? I can find no discussion at all on the bill. Talk about the reform of the senate; they are here today and away tomorrow! They are on holidays now. We know nothing about these bills.
The committee system of this house might as well be abolished. I do not wish to reflect on the mover of the bill because he is an honoured member. I have a copy of the bill here, and I must say that I cannot understand why it was not introduced in the House of Commons where sit the representatives of the different constituencies, not only in the province of Quebec for which I have a great respect, but in the whole of Canada. Where is the report of the superintendent of insurance on this bill?
The company is being given power to trans-sact .fire insurance, accident insurance, aircraft insurance, automobile insurance, boiler insurance, credit insurance, and so forth. We have

had a dozen of these bills in the last few years. There are too many of them. The company can also transact earthquake insurance, explosion insurance, livestock insurance, marine insurance, personal property insurance and many other things. I proposed three years ago that we should have a body similar to the board of transport commissioners to look after these fire and life insurance companies and many others. There was an investigation made into these companies in 1929 or 1930. Many of them could not qualify for a certificate under the law. Many of them are purely provincial companies, and they are taking advantage of the senate to introduce the bills over there. The thing is becoming a racket. That is what I called it three or four years ago. If this house is to be flooded with bills of this kind, we are on very dangerous ground. There are too many of these companies. They pile up. Later, by some merger they come in and get a charter and float it all around the country; then they come back, and sooneT or later we find that it is gobbled up by some larger concern. If this is the way in which the House of Commons is conducting its business we are on very dangerous ground.

I am going to have a few words to say on this bill. I imagine that this is a dangerous field to get into. I agree with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) who has just taken his seat that the other place is beginning to initiate too much legislation. I notice that most of the bills which come from the other place deal with million dollar corporations. Without giving hon. members of this house, or a committee of this house, an opportunity to go over these bills and have some understanding of the intentions of the people who are sponsoring them, they are thrown at us at a moment's notice and we are obliged to make a decision on them. The first objection I have is that if the other place is to continue to initiate legislation of this kind some provision must be made for a committee of the House of Commons at least to scrutinize these bills before they come to this house.
I am glad to see that the hon. member for Broadview is about seventy-five per cent socialist when he suggests that if this field is still open some move should be made by the government to set up some supervisory machinery to give the government some control over it. This bill is all right; it is innocent-looking enough; the capitalization is not too great.

Of the worker.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the principle underlying this bill is exactly the same as that of the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association which was read a second time a few moments ago. I may say that optometry is perhaps the youngest profession we have in Canada, since it has existed as a body only since the beginning of this century. In 1909 by letters patent the Ontario association was incorporated. Since then, each and all of the provincial associations have become organized by provincial statute to regulate the admission to and the practice of optometry within their borders. I do not think there is much more that I can say at this time. It would be more in order to wait until the committee stage to give any particulars on the sections of the bill.

Here is a bill which is not by the widest stretch of the imagination a federal bill or for the general advantage of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on this bill. My deskmate, who was speaking when the debate was adjourned last Friday, is unfortunately unable to be here tonight and I should like to continue for a few minutes what he really intended to say.
The first fact that strikes one on looking into this bill is the tremendous amount of money that is involved. I do not understand why so much money is needed. Perhaps one of the things that attracted my attention to the bill in the first place was the speech of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mae-Nicol) and the speech of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), men who have spent a lifetime in the public service and who, when it comes to transportation, hydro, communications, and even irrigation take second place to no one. The bill has been pretty well discussed. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) pointed out the manner in which the company had divided up the shares, a thing that always creates suspicion in the minds of the rank and file when one sees a large company doing such a thing.
I do not understand why a bill like this, so important to the whole dominion, should not be brought in by the government instead of being left to be introduced by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret).
Because it is a private company.
The hon. member for Outremont has my sympathy in being asked to sponsor a bill like this one.
You mean that with your help it will be better?
Do not feel sorry for a lawyer.

Do not feel sorry for a
person introducing a bill like this.

I was going to say, when I was interrupted by the independent member, that the bill should have been brought in by the government. I think that was the right and proper thing to do. When a company's capital is to be increased from $150,000,000 to $500,000,000, that is something which should be done on the floor of this house so that we can get into it. I have supported public
ownership most of my life. I think the telephone system should be under public ownership, and the service should be given at cost because it is something that every individual can use. When you stop to figure this out, you find that power is to be given to a private company to bring its capitalization up to $500 million. By giving that power, you are only helping to build up a great private monopoly. No doubt the greatest weakness in the free enterprise system today is the tendency for private companies to grow into monopolies.
The Bell Telephone Company now has a capitalization of $150,000.

$150 million.
Bell Telephone Company

I get mixed up in this, Mr. Speaker, because I have never been accustomed to talking in figures like that. I understand that the Bell Telephone Company was started or incorporated in 1880. The capital allowed was $1,000,000 at that time. In 1884 the capitalization was raised to $2,000,000. In 1892 it was again raised to $5,000,000. In 1902 it was advanced to $10,000,000. In 1906 they were allowed to increase the capitalization to $30,000,000. In 1920 the capitalization was increased to $75,000,000 and, in 1929, to $150 million. Now we have this bill asking that the capital be increased to $500 million which seems to me to be out of all proportion. Had they asked for $100 million or something reasonable, it would be different. But when they ask for $500 million, I do not know what to make of it.
They might as well take over the national debt.
I should have liked to know what they are going to use that money for.
Let the bill go to the committee.

I have been thinking this matter over since it has been debated in the house. I wonder if this money is for the purpose of allowing them to by-pass the provincial telephones, in some way for the Bell Telephone Company to be able to dictate to the provincial governments in the prairie provinces? Had we been able to go to committee, I could ask that question. I cannot get any answer to it today. The hon. member who is sponsoring the bill does not say whether that is so or whether it is not. If that is the case, that the Bell Telephone Company is getting this money so as to put a direct line through the United States in order to by-pass the prairie provinces, it is a shame if this government or this parliament should give it authority to get that money.
I explained why it was. Read my speech.

Read my speech.

Mr. Speaker tells me not to answer.

A most reliable publication is Moody's. I looked up Moody's and the Lehigh railway operates 1,254 miles of railway track, the main line extending from New York to Buffalo. The last statement I could find in Moody's was that the capitalization was $170,000 per mile of track, which would give an over-all capitalization of $225 million. Most hon. members have seen that railway. They have a capitalization of only $225 million. Yet this company is asking for $500 million. Again I cannot help but regret that we have not had an opportunity to find out what this money is for. I think the telephone should be one of the public services, the same as our hydro and transportation lines. Businesses such as these should be run as a service, at cost, and should not be used for private gain. The telephone is a necessary service to the people and should be operated for the good of all. A bill like this asking for large sums of money for capital expansion should not be brought in by a private member but by the government and should be given far more serious consideration than we have the opportunity of giving it here. My main objection to the bill is that it will create for this company a monopoly of a public service, namely, the telephone service.
Does the transport board not have jurisdiction in those matters?

This is the only time we as members of parliament have jurisdiction over the matter, and I think it is our duty to investigate all the ramifications. I am not quite sure as to the powers of the board of transport commissioners; but, as I said during the debate on freight rates, I am not any too pleased with the report of that board and its decision to permit that freight rate increase. So I am convinced that we as members of parliament have a real duty to perform in doing the best we can to make sure that our people get the best possible service at the lowest possible cost.
As the hon. member for Broadview has indicated, this bill went through the other place with practically no discussion at all. I do not think that is what should be done here.
I believe we should try to get all the information we can; but, despite the attempts of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) and others who have tried to get information from the sponsor of this bill, as yet we have not been given any information which would warrant us in approving an increase of over 230 per cent in the capitalization of a company of this kind. But what I say is this, that we are here as representatives of the people to look after the people's welfare. And when we find1 a monopoly, such as we now have in connection with fertilizers, and as we shall have in the Bell Telephone system, there is no assurance that our people will get, at reasonable prices, either the service or the goods they need. I am not so sure that I am quite satisfied with this arrangement. I remember very well the difficulty we had in having this board set up in the first place, and I have had considerable to do with it since it was set up. I want to pay tribute to that board. It is one section of the Department of Veterans Affairs which has performed yeoman service in a very difficult field. At the end of the war a large number of Canadian service personnel came back with misconduct discharges, in many cases for a very slight infraction of military rules and regulations, for which they were penalized severely. A misconduct discharge meant a stigma on a man for the rest of his life and militated against his securing employment. In addition many of them were fined and lost their pay and gratuity. We did not argue that they should be paid gratuity for the days or months they may have spent in confinement, but we did think that the gratuity should be paid for the period of actual service. That was not the case when the war ended and we brought the matter up in the house and in the veterans affairs committee. I was particularly active in the matter myself because I had a number of these cases on my hands. Ultimately the board was set up.
I Mr. Gregg.]
I agree with the minister that there is a saturation point in this kind of thing and that there may not be any longer the necessity of maintaining a full-time organization. But the board the minister is going to set up will consist of three or four or five officials of the department who already have a full-time job, and to whom this will be a sideline. They will be somewhat in the position of a broker in the city of Toronto who is also a member of parliament but whose mind is mostly on his private business rather than on the business here. Similarly the officials of the department will have their own specific work to do in the department, and this other work will be a sideline to them. I should like to know from the minister, before we pass this amendment, how many misconduct discharges there were, how many applications were made to the board, how many were granted and how many refused. Then we shall have some idea of the number still to be dealt with. I believe there is still a large number who have not made application for the gratuity which I think will be coming to them under the changes made in the War Service Grants Act.

If the minister can give us that information I would very much appreciate having it, because I am not prepared to disband the present board until I am reasonably sure that there is not sufficient work to keep them employed for some time to come.

speechtext: Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved the second reading of Bill No. 60, to amend the Veterans Insurance Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBILITY, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBILITY, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the main purpose of this bill to amend the Veterans Insurance Act is to extend and clarify the eligibility section of the act. This amendment is the first amending legislation that has been proposed since the act came into effect on February 20, 1945.
The original act provided for the approval of applications within three years after discharge or three years after the coming into force of the act. This bill provides for an extension of the period to six years. This will be of value especially to veterans who are still under treatment, or whose health at present will not permit their acceptance for insurance.
There are also veterans who are, or who have been, under training, and others who
Veterans Insurance Act

have been unable, for various reasons, to rehabilitate themselves financially, and they will welcome this extension. In addition there will be certain United States veterans who served in the Canadian forces who have been training under their G.I. bill of rights, and eventually they will be able to purchase veterans insurance with the remaining portion of their re-establishment credit.
The bill provides a revised and clarified definition of classes eligible to contract for insurance, and includes statutory provision for members of the permanent force and certain merchant seamen who originally qualified under ol der in council passed under emergency legislation, which has now expired. The bill will extend the benefits of the act to merchant seamen who qualified to receive a war service bonus. It excludes one small class, the dependent parents of deceased members of the forces, or persons standing in the place of parents. It was not intended that they should be eligible, but the phrasing of the act was found not clear, and this amendment includes a clarification of that.
Widows of members of the forces who died on service have previously qualified as pensioners. It is considered advisable to provide specifically that these widows shall qualify as widows, as do the widows of those who died after discharge. The class of pensioners will now include only those in receipt of a disability pension. _
The bill provides a clarification of wording in several places; there is also a retroactive feature which will avoid any break in the period of eligibility.
The total amount of veterans insurance issued to March 31, 1948, was 19,280 policies for $55,353,500 worth of insurance. There are some 211 applications now pending for $509,000 worth of insurance from veterans whose period of eligibility has already expired and, if this amendment is passed, who would become eligible.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS

speechtext:
Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Veterans Rehabilitation Act by extending the allowance provisions in respect to persons coming under the provisions of the act.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext: May we have a statement from the minister?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The resolution before the house, Mr. Speaker, is one dealing with amendments to the Veterans Rehabilitation Act. Certain anomalies and conflictions have occurred in the experience with that act since it first came upon the statute books, and in some respects these amendments are to correct those anomalies and conflictions which are based upon the experience of the department.
The bill-if I have your permission, Mr. Speaker, so to refer to it at this stage-will provide for the payment of allowances to veterans on behalf of children who are in the process of adoption. It will also provide for payment of an allowance where an illegitimate child of a veteran's wife is maintained by the veteran. Items such as these are taken up in the amendments.
Provision is contained in the oncoming bill to provide compensation to veteran trainees who received a disability from accidents which occurred during the course of their training subsequently to August 31, 1946. For example, one veteran suffered injury during his training prior to this date and is becoming blind as a result of the accident. The amendments proposed will take care of such cases prior to that date and will cover all cases of injury incurred during training, under the provisions of either the post-discharge re-establishment order or the Veterans Rehabilitation Act.
It has been ruled that an individual who enlisted during the war and remained with the permanent force and is finally discharged ten or twenty years hence will be eligible under the present legislation to apply for benefits under the Veterans Rehabilitation Act. I am told, Mr. Speaker, that that is something which was not in any way intended when the original act was passed; and from reading of the records I believe that is so. That will be corrected.
The intent of the act was to provide assistance for veterans on discharge from their war service. The proposed amendments in the

Veterans Rehabilitation Act
bill will provide that veterans of the permanent force will be deemed to have been discharged or retired from the forces as of September 30, 1947, which is in accord with order in council P.C. 2372 of June 17, 1947, whereby the armed forces ceased to be on active service after September 30, 1947.
Certain limitations are provided in the act which prevent desirable transfers from vocational training to university training, and the other way around. Perhaps this will be the most important feature of the legislation coming forward under this resolution. Cases have been brought to the attention of the department where these restrictions work a hardship on the veteran in his efforts to complete his rehabilitation. The oncoming amendments will permit transfers to take place for those who have discontinued training within six months of the coming into force of this amending legislation and for those now in training within six months from the date that they discontinued their present courses.
Also veterans who are receiving university training, including pre-matriculation courses leading up to university training, are debarred from the benefits of the Veterans Land Act. In many cases, because of a change in objective, the veteran, after completing his pre-matriculation course, did not continue on to university as he originally intended. The proposed amendments restore to such veteran students eligibility to apply for benefits under the Veterans Land Act. Where a veteran has completed one academic year of not more than nine months at. a university, he is required to pay the allowances and other costs of such training prior to the restoration of his entitlement under the Veterans Land Act.
These proposed amendments bring into effect the results of the experience of the department during the past three years in the preparation of veterans for their careers in life. Quite often they came out of the services convinced that they knew exactly what they were going to do in life and the course they wanted to follow to prepare for that objective. They had counsellors within the service; they had counsellors within the universities and vocational schools; they had counsellors in the department. Sometimes they thought they were counselled to death. However, in the main the veteran himself or herself made the decision. Sometimes the counselling had effect; sometimes it had not. After they got under way for a few months in vocational or university or on the job training, they found that was not the field they should try to enter, and, under the original act there was a certain rigidity that
made it difficult for such a veteran to take the fork in the road leading, the department hopes, to the vocation which best fits his aptitude.
This resolution gives me an opportunity tc say a word about the training program for veterans made possible by the original rehabilitation act. The number of veterans who have received or are receiving or are about to receive training at universities now stands at upwards of 55,000. When I say "are about to receive" I mean including those who are now at pre-matriculation schools with the intention of going on to universities. Therefore, including those who have graduated, those who are in, those who intend and are preparing to go in, the figure is over 55,000 at present. The corresponding total with regard to vocational training is approximately 93,000.
These numbers do not by any means tell the whole story. For example, when the original act came into effect the universities were faced with a great opportunity and a great duty to provide university training for veterans, which brought total enrolments at those universities up to two, three and, in one case in the far west, four times the normal enrolment. The story of how that has been done is an interesting one. It is a story of co-operation between the universities and the federal government in a way that has been a source of great satisfaction to the universities and which has been very effective in behalf of the veterans whom they tried to serve by leading them into the proper courses and eventually to rehabilitation.
The word "rehabilitation" was, of course, the key word. It was intended to give the student an opportunity to find his way back to civil life, but I am glad to say it is meaning more than that, Veterans at our universities, as well as those taking vocational training, are getting a broadening of experience and education that will mean more than mere rehabilitation, important though that may be. The initiative taken by the university authorities is leaving nothing undone, even changing the whole set-up of their establishments, to fit into this plan has been commendable. One pleasant feature is that it is being done with the universities maintaining their time-honoured autonomy, yet preserving the most harmonious relations with this department on the many interlocking points of operation that have come up.
I could say more on that point, but the amendments being brought in come within that field of co-operation. When the plan for university work came into operation each institution worked out, under university authority, a counselling service. Some of these services
5849-195J
Veterans Rehabilitation Act

have grown to quite extraordinary dimensions and are now considered to be an important part of university work. It was to a great degree through that counselling, after the student veteran got under way, that this need for redirection of course became more apparent. All the universities operating under the plan have that system in effect now, and it has been possible for them to do that without interference by the department, while at the same time receiving from the department assistance under their supplementary grants making this possible.
The amendments being brought forward, providing as they do more flexibility in the early direction of courses, are a direct result of that work, and I am sure that the experience gained in this field by the universities will be of value long after the veteran period has passed, that it will be one of the useful byproducts. I could say much also about the task involved in working out the vocational training for the nearly ninety-five thousand veterans concerned.
In some cases, particularly in medicine and dentistry, the fees to the university plus the supplementary grant of $150 have exceeded the $500 which it will be remembered the act set as the maximum payable on behalf of the veteran in tuition fees. The ratio of costs of instruction in medicine and dentistry has increased to a greater extent than in practically all the other courses. As hon. members know, Canada is very short of medical men and dentists, and a great many veterans elected to take those courses. So an attempt is made here to see that no potential veteran doctor or veteran dentist does not take the course due to the fact that his tuition is more than $500. In other words, an attempt is made to have that tuition payable on his behalf.

The overseas wife of a Canadian veteran can get a divorce in England by proving desertion, but that divorce does not hold good in Canada. .1 hope, if my interpretation of the minister's statement is correct, that he will give the matter serious consideration, because it seems to me that a condition of that kind would be doing a gross injustice to those men who are still remaining on in the service of this country. Completing his course, he found that he could not get a job, and as a result made application for unemployment insurance. However, he could not estab-

Veterans Rehabilitation Act
lish a benefit year and had not made the 180 contributions. Then he applies for his armed service credits, which are applicable in a case of this kind to any serviceman who did not take a course.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the passage of the resolution for any length of time. The minister referred to university students and to vocational training and, I believe, made the suggestion that possibly some of these students have not been getting their training along lines best suited to them. His suggestion that a change should now be made is a good one.
There is another class of student to whom very little attention has been paid. I refer to children of veterans who were killed overseas or who were war casualties. Mr. HOWARD C. GREEN (Vancouver South): Mr. Speaker, there are two or three matters I should like to place before the minister and the house in connection with rehabilitation. As I understand it, this measure does not apply to veterans of the first world war. When I was in Vancouver during the Easter recess I found that there are some veterans of the first war around the age of
fifty years who could be benefited greatly by receiving vocational training of one kind or another. I have in mind training as gardeners. Apparently some of them have had that training and have been enabled to get jobs from which they are able to earn a living.
The minister's staff in Vancouver has no authority to give training of that kind to veterans of the first war. Incidentally, in my opinion the staff in Vancouver-and I have no doubt the same condition obtains elsewhere-are doing a fine job in helping to place veterans of both the first and second world wars. Another group I would mention is that of the merchant seamen. In his opening remarks the minister said nothing about extending the benefits of rehabilitation to the merchant seamen. My understanding is that the only benefits they can get now are by way of training for the sea. They can get vocational training to go to sea, but not otherwise. For example, they cannot get training at a university. As the house knows, our merchant marine is small in size, although it is a great deal larger than it was before the war. Yet it is so small, compared with its size during the war, that only a very small proportion of the men who served in the merchant navy could hope to carry on in that occupation in peacetime.
In effect, most of the men who served in the merchant navy can get no rehabilitation benefits, and I hope that the government has not closed the door on giving training to these men. The minister said nothing with regard to university students. The married students were given an increase of, I believe, $10 a month, but there was no increase whatever given to the single students, and the representations that I receive are to the effect that
Veterans Rehabilitation Act

$10 a month is still not sufficient to meet the requirements of the married men. The single men are getting in a worse position all the time. The cost of living has been going up steadily; the funds of these men are running lower and lower, and many of them are going deeper and deeper into debt. I would ask the minister to explain just what the situation is in- that regard. There are one or two points to which I might refer while on my feet. One was with regard to divorce. I am going to leave that to the veterans affairs committee. Like other members of that committee, I have run across difficult situations, and if a solution can be found I shall be as happy as anyone.
Referring to the point made by the hon. member for Nanaimo, I said a little while ago that my understanding of the purpose of the original rehabilitation act was to have the veteran re-established. As we stand now, it would appear to me that the permanent officer or soldier is re-established. If by any chance he is discharged now or next week or next year he will, of course, come under whatever remaining benefits there may be related to the last war, but twenty years from now one would expect that vocational training schools and university training plans and many of these other things which were built up definitely for re-establishment will have served their purpose. speechtext:
I suppose I am going to be quite out of order. I have listened to some of the debate which has gone on, and I think this might be a constructive suggestion. We have quite a lot of difficulty at the present time in getting volunteers for the navy, army and air force. We are below strength. Under the circumstances today, Canada should do something to see that she is able to defend herself. My suggestion is that in Canada at the present time we should have universal volunteer training. I do not know what I should suggest as the length of time that we should have it. I suggest perhaps a year or a year and a half. During that year or a year and.a half we should have universal volunteer training. This is not conscription or anything like that. We should take into the navy, army and air force men who have finished their high school courses or perhaps those who have finished their first year course at the
Veterans Rehabilitation Act

university. I suggest to the minister, who knows something about education, that perhaps it is a wise thing to have a boy go to university for one year and then go out and earn his living and come back to university. That system would give him a better understanding of what earning a dollar means.
My suggestion is that we formulate some plan for the defence of Canada and that we give these boys, during the period of their voluntary training, schooling which will be equivalent to whatever year they are in in high school or matriculation or something like that. If they are in arts they could carry on the first year of arts or the first year of science. Give them something that will carry them along that year and make it worthwhile. It will take a lot of money, but if we do that we shall get the voluntary force which will be needed to defend Canada in case of necessity. I want to repeat that this is voluntary.
One of the main reasons I have for speaking about this matter tonight is this. We have the threat of communism on us in Canada today. What we must have in Canada as soon as we can get it, to combat any subservient activity which may come along, is loyal subjects. We must have people who voluntarily are willing to defend their country in time of trouble. I am not talking about having them voluntarily defend their country in time of war outside Canada. That goes without saying, because we know that every man, woman and child in this country, in the case of war, outside, would jump into the fray and defend Canada.

On the point raised regarding student veterans at universities, I am not going to discuss that at any length, except to say that across Canada there is a great variation in costs just as there is a great variation in the thriftiness of the students

Veterans Rehabilitation Act
themselves. As I understood it-I may have been wrong-this plan was developed as an effective federal scholarship for veteran students. Let us take the maximum, or less than the maximum. The maximum tuition has been $500 and, if it is more now, it will be paid, but the average tuition across Canada is in the vicinity of $300. There is $60 a month for a normal eight months period, which is $480. So that the veteran has a scholarship of $300, plus $480, or $780, and that applies, whether he is single or married, to the veteran himself.
This increase was designed to assist the married veteran and to make it more possible for him as a married man to take care of his dependents. True, he did not have to get married, but to my mind it is a great advantage to the country that the young men who are at the universities are finding it in the main possible to get married and to have children; and I 'believe that when they come through with their war service and their university training, together with their initiation in domestic experience, they will be valuable citizens.
I know that in some parts of Canada, in the large centres, there is some hardship even yet for some individual married students, and there is as well, in some cases, for single students. The single student is able at this time of the year, or he will be in a few weeks' time, to reduce his expenses and his responsibilities. He can go and work for the whole summer. He can get work of some kind, quite often along the lines of his expected profession, and he is.able to return in the autumn with at least some surplus money to act as a backlog for the coming session at the university.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext: I think it is more difficult this year.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext: It is more difficult for them to get the type of work that is closely related to their university training, but there is work that can be got which would enable the single man to make a good deal more than it will cost him to live. On the other hand, the married man has to retain an establishment somewhere, normally at the place which he has found, or which has been found for him, within the university precincts or within the university community. Failing this, he has to send his small family home, which costs money. It is a rare case in which the married student veteran can get through the long summer holiday with very much of a surplus for the coming year.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext: What are the reports as to summer work for students this year? Will there be 100 per cent work obtainable, or what is the proportion?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
We have not had any definite reports in that regard and we shall not have until the holidays begin, 'because there is a great deal of last-minute employment. There is the closest possible co-operation between the labour department, through the employment offices across Canada, and the counselling service within the universities, which normally has, as a part of the service, a full-fledged employment bureau. The Department of Labour often has in the larger universities a full-time, or, in the smaller universities, a part-time representative meshed in with the university employment office, upon which normally the students' representative council has a quota of representatives. This assists in placing students.
There are sent from Ottawa through the employment offices of the Department of Labour to the universities lists of opportunities for summer employment. Instead of their being posted up casually, they are studied by the employment officers of the university and the students' representatives. The veterans affairs representative also has a part in the work with the Department of Labour. An attempt is being made to sort out the summer opportunities to fit the type of training the veteran student is taking, so that, if it is engineering he is taking, for example, he may get some kind of work related to engineering, and so on. I must admit that the opportunities in the applied science field are much greater than they are in the field of pure arts and science.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext: What about the permissible earnings?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The permissible earnings still stand at $75 a month for the veteran. A married man may earn $75 a month and his wife may earn $75 a month. But those restrictions apply, of course, only while he is actually at the university, or approximately eight months a year. The reason this was set up was, I think, to assist the student to keep in mind the importance of what he was doing, that the task he was undertaking at the university had the topmost priority, that his work there under the assistance of the government was important and the help he received was intended to assist him to get his training in the shortest possible time, rather than that he should be employed in the town and that the university work should be of secondary consideration.
Veterans Rehabilitation Act

I should like to add one other factor and that is that for any veteran student, in an emergency, there is still available a loan to keep him, if he is a good student, from having to leave on account of financial shortage.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext: Apparently the students do not like to go into debt.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext: Nobody does.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I believe there is a great reluctance among the students to incur indebtedness in order to finance their courses. Surely the department has control over the progress made by students. I think that is one of the features of the whole plan. If the veteran does good work, if he gets within a certain percentage or is fairly close to the top, he can get the benefit of a longer period than his service calls for. I think there is an effective check on the work being done by the students in universities. I doubt whether it is necessary to restrict the amount they may earn. In some cases the veteran or the veteran's wife might well be able to earn enough money to make it a great deal easier for the family to get by.
Another point is this. If this training is in the nature of a scholarship, there should be no ceiling placed on earnings. You do not say to a scholarship holder that he can earn only so much out of his university time. I cannot see why it should be necessary to impose these restrictions on earnings, and I would ask the minister to give some consideration to removing them.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10. respecting the appointment of auditors for national railways.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the annual bill seeking the appointment of auditors for the Canadian National Railways. The firm of George A. Touche and Company, chartered accountants, with offices in Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and other cities, have been appointed for the last number of years and have been doing the work of the Canadian National Railways with satisfaction. There are many advantages in having a continuous accounting of the affairs of the railways, and it would be inconvenient if the auditors were changed, because the work must be of a continuing nature. Again for the year 1948 this bill seeks the appointment of the same firm of auditors.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: I should like to draw the attention of the house to the debate that took place a year ago when a similar resolution was under consideration, during which the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) made what I considered a very reasonable argument with a view to having this important work done under the direction of the auditor general rather than by this particular firm of chartered accountants. I have had some contact with this firm since I have been a member of the committee that has examined the operations of the Canadian National Railways, and I have no criticism whatever to offer with respect to the auditing that has been done by the George A. Touche Company. But, as the hon. member for Vancouver North argued a year ago, there is no good reason why this work might not be undertaken and completed by the auditor general. Last year the minister gave the reasons he thought were important, but I do not think the defence made by the minister was very reasonable.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: The house agreed with it.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
Yes, the house did agree with it; but I think no great problem presents itself in asking the auditor general to take over the job. The book-keeping of the Canadian National Railways has been done very carefully over a period of years, and there is no
reason under the sun why the staff of the auditor general could not perform this service. I feel that the views we expressed a year ago apply with equal force this year. I draw Your Honour's attention to the amendment I moved a year ago, which is found at page 1910 of Hansard for March 31, 1947. At that time I referred you to page 228 of Beauchesne, third edition, citation 657, which was my authority for moving the amendment. So this evening I would move an amendment in exactly the same terms, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the making of provision for the auditing of the accounts of the Canadian National Railways to be done by the auditor general of Canada."

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say a word im reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). I need mot amplify what was said on the subject last year, but I am surprised that the hon. member should move the same, amendment, giving the same reasons, w'hen the amendment was defeated last year.
The reasons that it would not be in the public interest to have the auditor general audit the accounts of the Canadian National Railways are, first of all, that the auditing should be a continuing process. If the auditor general were to do the work he would have to set up a specific and separate staff to look after the special work of the railway. Again, the Canadian National Railways have offices in the United States. George A. Touche and Company have offices in various centres of the United States where the Canadian National Railways operate, and by means of these representatives are able to do the work far more efficiently than the auditor general could. I understand that a staff of some thirty or forty are assigned to the Canadian National Railways, of whom many attend exclusively to this particular job of auditing. The auditor general would be in exactly the same position and would have to employ a separate staff.
For these reasons and many others I gave during the debate last year, I think it would be against the public interest to have auditors other than the present firm, who have given entire satisfaction to the railways and, I think, to parliament as a whole.
Amendment (Mr. Nicholson) negatived on division.

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to increase the amount to be appropriated for the railway grade crossing fund from $200,000 to $500,000 each year for nine years, commencing on the first day of April, 1948,
He said:
The object of this resolution is to increase from 8200,000 to 8500,000 the amount paid into the grade crossing fund. Last year, 1947, there was passed an amendment to the Railway Act which provided for the payment into the railway grade crossing fund for a period of ten years an annual amount of 8200,000. It has been thought advisable in 1948 to increase the payment from 8200,000 to 8500,000, because there are many projects now before the board of transport commissioners, involving large grants from the fund. It was felt that, with the grade crossing fund standing at the amount at which it was during the greater part of 1947, and again in 1948, the appropriation should be increased. There are, of course, special votes which are made from time to time by the house, which have to do with special projects involving grade crossing features.
This resolution will seek not only to increase the appropriation to the grade crossing fund but to amend the Railway Act in perhaps three or four different ways. They are amendments which have to do with the construction of
cables under highways, with giving to the board the same powers in all municipalities which it has in towns and cities, and two other minor amendments which I need not discuss until we are in committee on the bill.
